1240.title: Dogen's instructions for sitting
1240.hook: Dogen's short guide to zazen: sit, let go, don't think of good or bad
1240.howItsDone: Soto Zen communities chant or read Dogen's Fukanzazengi, his short guide to zazen, and teachers use it to introduce posture and the attitude of sitting without judging thoughts as good or bad.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dogen's instructions for the cook, rice and water treated as carefully as your own eyes. Your line: as your own eyes.

It opens with a question that could end the whole project before it starts. If the way is already complete, everywhere, why would anyone need to practice? If it's never been lost, why sit down to find it? That's how Dogen begins his short guide to zazen. He doesn't wave the question away. He answers with a warning: the smallest gap between you and the way, and they're as far apart as heaven and earth. Then he tells you exactly what to do with your body and your mind.
screen: `IF THE WAY IS COMPLETE, WHY SIT?` → `THE SMALLEST GAP.` → `WHAT TO DO WITH BODY AND MIND.`

segments.voice: First, a recommendation for everyone. In Japanese the title is Fukanzazengi, rendered as a universal recommendation for zazen. Universal is the point: it's offered to everyone, not only to monks. Second, set down every involvement. He says, in paraphrase: put aside all your involvements, let every affair rest. A quiet room, moderate food and drink, a thick mat, a cushion. Then the posture you met earlier on this path: legs crossed or settled, hands in the oval, back upright, eyes open. Sway a little left and right, then settle into steady, unmoving sitting. Third, non-thinking. Don't think about good or bad, he says in paraphrase; don't judge right or wrong. Stop measuring. Then the turn. Think of not-thinking. How do you think of not-thinking? Non-thinking. It sounds like a riddle, and readers still discuss it. One plain reading: you don't fight thoughts, and you don't follow them. A thought arises, you notice it, and it goes on its way. Not forcing the mind blank; letting go of the grip. Fourth, the gate of ease and joy. Zazen, Dogen says in paraphrase, isn't a technique for learning meditation. It's the gate of ease and joy, practice and awakening in one. That answers his opening question: you don't practice because the way is missing. You practice because practice is how the way shows up.

segments.voice: Settle your body, then sway gently left and right, smaller each time, until you're still, hands resting and eyes half open. Then take Dogen's instruction for the mind: when a thought comes, don't call it good or bad. Notice it, and let it go on its way.
Dogen's instructions for sitting. His short guide to zazen: set everything down, sit upright and still, don't think of good or bad, and let thoughts go. Today's word.
Your line: let go. Not a blank mind, just a looser grip. See you at the next sitting.

1241.title: Mountains walking
1241.hook: Dogen's teaching that the blue mountains are always walking
1241.howItsDone: Zen students read Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra (Sansuikyo) from the Shobogenzo, often in study groups, and teachers return to its line about the walking mountains to unsettle fixed ways of seeing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dogen's guide to zazen, settling into steady, unmoving sitting and letting thoughts go. Your line: let go.

A mountain is the stock picture of something that doesn't move. People say steady as a mountain. So it's startling to open another of Dogen's essays, the Mountains and Waters Sutra, and find him passing on an old Chan teacher's saying, in paraphrase: the blue mountains are always walking. Not once, long ago. Always. And then he turns it on the reader.
screen: `STEADY AS A MOUNTAIN.` → `THE BLUE MOUNTAINS ARE ALWAYS WALKING.` → `THEN HE TURNS IT ON YOU.`

segments.voice: First, where it comes from. Dogen quotes the line from an earlier Chan teacher, Furong Daokai, and builds an essay around it. The essay is part of his larger collection, the Shobogenzo. Second, what he says about it. In paraphrase: the mountains' walking is just like people's walking; don't doubt it because it doesn't look like human walking. Then the turn: if you doubt the mountains walking, you don't yet understand your own walking. The puzzle isn't really about rocks. It's about how you see anything at all. Third, time, or a habit of seeing? Readers hear it more than one way. Some hear it about time: the mountain you're looking at is never quite the same mountain twice. Wind, water, seasons and light move through it, and it moves through them. Some hear it about seeing: the idea that a mountain sits still while you're the one going places is a habit of the mind, not the whole truth. Dogen doesn't settle it with a single explanation. He keeps the line strange on purpose. Fourth, what looks fixed is still moving. It's easy to treat certain things as fixed: a parent, a hometown, a job, one's own personality. That's just how it is. This teaching gently loosens that. What looks fixed may be quietly moving. And the self that thinks it's the only thing on the road may be standing still more than it knows.
screen: `AN OLD CHAN LINE, A DOGEN ESSAY.` · `DOUBT THE MOUNTAINS, DOUBT YOUR WALK.` · `TIME, OR A HABIT OF SEEING?` · `WHAT LOOKS FIXED IS STILL MOVING.` · then, large: `THE MOUNTAINS WALK.`

segments.voice: Rest your eyes on a hill, a tree, a building or even a wall, or picture a mountain you've seen, and let it be still. Then slowly notice what is moving in it or through it: light changing, air, shadows, the life on it, the way your own looking shifts. Don't decide what it means; just wonder, as Dogen invites: is it walking?

1242.title: A man up a tree
1242.hook: a man hangs from a branch by his teeth; someone asks why Bodhidharma came west (Gateless Gate 5)
1242.howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen, students are given koans such as this one to hold through sitting and daily life, and they present their response to the teacher in private interview rather than writing an answer down.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dogen's blue mountains: what looks still is quietly walking. Your line: the mountains walk.

A man is up a tree, hanging from a branch by his teeth. His hands grip nothing. His feet touch nothing. Below him, a long drop. And someone under the tree calls up a question: why did Bodhidharma come from the west? It's a question Zen stories use to ask what this whole tradition is about. If the man keeps quiet, he fails the person asking. If he opens his mouth to answer, he falls. That's the whole story, case five of the Gateless Gate, and it ends with a question for you: what would you do?
screen: `HANGING BY HIS TEETH.` → `A QUESTION FROM BELOW.` → `SPEAK AND FALL. STAY SILENT AND FAIL.`

segments.voice: Back in year one, a koan was a short story or question meant to stop the thinking mind. Here is one at full squeeze. First, who tells it: a teacher named Xiangyan, Kyogen in Japanese. He sets up the scene and stops. He never says what the man did; the koan hands the problem to whoever is listening. Second, the trap. Answer, and you fall. Don't, and you've turned away someone who asked the biggest thing they could ask. The mind hunts for a third door: shout, nod, hum through your teeth. A clever escape misses the point. This isn't a riddle with a trick answer. It's built to leave thinking with nowhere to stand. Third, why a tree. This week's koans each carry some version of this pressure, and here there are no free hands and no ground. That's a picture of a moment any life can bring: a hospital hallway, a phone call, a choice where every road costs something. Zen students don't solve the case like a puzzle. They stay with the squeeze long enough to find out who is hanging there. Fourth, the comment. The compiler, Wumen, added a comment and a verse to each case. In paraphrase, he says even a flood of eloquence is no use here, and if you can answer in this spot, you bring dead things back to life. He doesn't hand over the answer either. Some readers notice the man is still alive at the end. The whole koan happens in one held breath, the teeth still holding.
screen: `XIANGYAN SETS IT UP AND STOPS.` · `BOTH DOORS LOOK LIKE LOSING.` · `NO HANDS, NO GROUND.` · `WUMEN: ELOQUENCE IS NO USE.` · then, large: `HANGING BY THE TEETH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one choice in your life where every option seems to cost something, and don't solve it or list pros and cons. Just hold it, the way the man holds the branch, and feel where the squeeze sits: the jaw, the chest, the hands. When the mind races for a third door, notice the racing and come back to the breath.
A man up a tree. Xiangyan's koan, case five of the Gateless Gate: hanging by the teeth, asked the great question, with no safe way to speak or stay silent. Today's word.

1243.title: "Master!"
1243.hook: Zuigan calls to himself each day, "Master!" and answers "Yes!" (Gateless Gate 12)
1243.howItsDone: Zen students may be given this case as a koan; some also take Ruiyan's habit as a simple reminder, pausing during the day to call themselves back to attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man hanging from a branch by his teeth, with a question coming from below. Your line: hanging by the teeth.

Somewhere in a monastery in old China, a monk calls out: Master! There's no one else he's calling. He answers himself: Yes! Then he goes on. Wake up! Yes! From now on, don't be fooled by anyone. Yes! Yes! The Gateless Gate says he did this every day. Zen keeps the story as case twelve: the monk who called his own name.

First, the man: Ruiyan, Zuigan in Japanese. The case gives one picture of him, a daily habit of calling out to himself and answering. Master here isn't a teacher across the room. It's the one inside, the one he's trying to rouse. Second, the three calls. The first is just a name: are you there? The second, wake up: be here, not half asleep in your own life. The third, don't be fooled by others, any day, any time. That could mean other people's opinions, or the stories the mind tells about itself. The case doesn't explain; he just answers, yes, yes. Third, the twist. Wumen, the compiler, isn't simply impressed. In paraphrase, he says old Ruiyan buys and sells himself, putting on a whole set of masks: one to call, one to answer, one awake, one that won't be fooled. Take any mask as the real thing, and you've missed it. Copy Ruiyan, Wumen says, and your understanding is like a fox's. So this isn't a tidy self-help trick; its own collector pokes at it. Fourth, why it stays. For long stretches of a day, attention runs on its own, like a car with nobody checking the road. Calling your own name taps the shoulder. Some readers hear Ruiyan's practice as kind: he doesn't scold himself, he just calls and answers yes. And the koan leaves the question underneath wide open: who is it that answers?

1244.title: Dongshan's three pounds of flax
1244.hook: asked what Buddha is, Dongshan answers: three pounds of flax (Gateless Gate 18)
1244.carry: no line between holy and plain
1244.howItsDone: Zen students may receive this case as a koan in Rinzai training, carrying the phrase through sitting and daily work and presenting their understanding in private interview with the teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruiyan called his own name each day and answered yes. Your line: wake up.

The question could hardly be bigger. A monk asks a teacher, straight out: what is Buddha? Not what did the Buddha teach, not where is he now. What is Buddha. And the teacher answers with something you could buy at a market stall: three pounds of flax. No explanation follows, no smile that lets you in on the joke. That's the whole case, number eighteen of the Gateless Gate, and Zen students still sit with it.
screen: `WHAT IS BUDDHA?` → `THREE POUNDS OF FLAX.` → `TWO LINES. NO EXPLANATION.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher: Dongshan, Tozan in Japanese. Not the founder of the Caodong line who shares the name; this is a different Dongshan, Dongshan Shouchu. Second, the answer. Flax is a plant fiber, what linen is made from. Three pounds of it is an ordinary weight of an ordinary thing, the sort of bundle a monastery might keep for cloth or robes. Some retellings picture Dongshan in the storehouse, weighing flax as the monk walks in. The case doesn't say so, and that's worth noticing: the plain answer comes with no setting to explain it away. Third, what the answer refuses. The monk wants a definition, and a definition would put Buddha in one place and flax in another, the holy here, the ordinary there. Dongshan doesn't draw that line. Some readers hear it pointing at what's right in front of you, nothing hidden. Others say any explanation, that one included, already misses, because the answer is meant to stop the mind that reaches for explanations. Fourth, Wumen's comment. In paraphrase, old Dongshan opened up like a clam, showing everything inside at once, and still people miss it. Completely exposed, completely ordinary. It hides nothing, and it can't be explained.
screen: `A DIFFERENT DONGSHAN.` · `FLAX: AN ORDINARY BUNDLE.` · `NO LINE BETWEEN HOLY AND PLAIN.` · `WUMEN: OPEN LIKE A CLAM.` · then, large: `THREE POUNDS OF FLAX.`

segments.voice: Pick up one ordinary thing near you, a mug, a phone, a shoe, an orange, and feel its weight: not what it's worth or what it's for, just how heavy it is, pressing into your palm. Then set it down and sit with the breath, letting the weight linger like an echo. If a thought comes to explain the koan, let it pass and come back to the weight.
Three pounds of flax. Dongshan's answer when a monk asked what Buddha is, case eighteen of the Gateless Gate: an ordinary weight of an ordinary thing. Today's word.

1245.title: The cypress tree
1245.hook: asked why Bodhidharma came, Zhaozhou answers: the cypress tree in the garden (Gateless Gate 37)
1245.howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen training this case is given as a koan, and students carry the phrase 'the cypress tree in front of the garden' through sitting and work until they can present it to the teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a monk asked what Buddha is, and Dongshan said: three pounds of flax. Your line: three pounds of flax.

Three days ago, a man hung from a tree by his teeth while someone asked why Bodhidharma came from the west. Today the question comes back, and this time it gets an answer. A monk puts it to Zhaozhou, the old Chan teacher you first met with his answer mu: why did Bodhidharma come from the west? Zhaozhou doesn't lecture or open a book. He points, as it were, out the window: the cypress tree in front of the garden. Case thirty-seven of the Gateless Gate is that short.
screen: `THE QUESTION COMES BACK.` → `ZHAOZHOU DOESN'T LECTURE.` → `THE CYPRESS TREE.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Tradition says Bodhidharma carried the Chan way from India to China, so asking why he came is asking what the whole tradition is for. It's the question the man in the tree was asked, and here a teacher answers it. Second, the answer. Zhaozhou names a tree in a courtyard, right there. Not a symbol, not a parable: a tree you could walk over and touch. Like the flax, it won't send the monk somewhere else for the meaning. The answer to the big question is standing in the yard. Third, a detail for the curious. The Chinese word names a cypress or juniper kind of tree, and some English versions call it an oak. So depending on your book, Zhaozhou points at a different tree. The koan doesn't seem to mind; whatever is in front of you is the point. Fourth, why it lands. Some questions in a life seem to need a faraway answer: a different job, a different city, a different self. Zhaozhou turns the head around. The tree was there before the question and will be there after it. In koan practice, the student isn't asked for an essay on trees, but to meet the tree, or whatever is in front of them, so fully that nothing is left over to explain.

segments.voice: Find one tree, out a window, down the street, or one you know well in memory, and look at it: the bark, the way the branches split, where the light hits. Don't name its species or think about what it stands for; just let it be a tree, in front of you, now. When the mind wanders, come back to the tree and breathe with it.
The cypress tree. Zhaozhou's answer when asked why Bodhidharma came from the west, case thirty-seven of the Gateless Gate: the tree in front of the garden. Today's word.

1246.title: The top of the pole
1246.hook: how do you step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole? (Gateless Gate 46)
1246.howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen this case is given as a koan, and teachers sometimes use the image of the pole's top to warn students against holding on to a calm or insight they have reached in sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhaozhou's answer to the biggest question: the cypress tree in front of the garden. Your line: the cypress in the garden. Today, the week closes.

This week opened with Dogen telling us how to sit, then saying the blue mountains walk. Then the koans, one a day: a man hanging by his teeth, a monk calling his own name, three pounds of flax, a cypress tree. Each took away somewhere to stand: no safe answer, no faraway meaning. Today's case goes all the way up. A teacher named Shishuang asks: from the top of a hundred-foot pole, how do you take one step forward?
screen: `DOGEN: SIT. THE MOUNTAINS WALK.` → `TEETH, A NAME, FLAX, A TREE.` → `NOW: A HUNDRED-FOOT POLE.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. A pole a hundred feet high, and someone who has climbed it all the way. Every hand over hand was real work. Now they're balanced at the top, sky all around, and Shishuang doesn't ask how you got here. He asks how you step forward from here, with no more pole to climb. Second, an older warning. The case adds the words of a teacher from long before. In paraphrase: someone sitting on top of the pole has got somewhere, but it isn't yet the real thing. They need one more step, showing their whole body in all ten directions. Third, why the top can be a trap. Some teachers read the top as an attainment you can hold onto: a calm you finally reached, a breakthrough in sitting, a self-image as someone who gets it. It feels like arriving, and the case says arriving is where you get stuck. Stepping off doesn't mean throwing practice away. Some readers hear it as letting go of the height itself and coming back down into the whole world, ordinary life included. Fourth, the week. The flax and the cypress said: it's right here. The pole says it from the other side. Even what you reached by climbing becomes a new place to cling. The koan asks for one more step, and leaves the stepping to you.
screen: `A HUNDRED-FOOT POLE, CLIMBED.` · `ONE MORE STEP, IN ALL DIRECTIONS.` · `THE TOP CAN BE A TRAP.` · `THE FLAX, THE TREE, THE POLE.` · then, large: `STEP OFF THE POLE.`

segments.voice: Think of one place you've climbed to and now hold tightly, a routine, a way of being seen, a comfort you guard, and notice without judging how your body holds it, in the shoulders or the jaw. Then, on an out-breath, picture loosening that grip by a single degree: one small step past comfort, not a leap. Rest there.
The top of the pole. Shishuang's question in case forty-six of the Gateless Gate: from the top of a hundred-foot pole, how do you step forward? Today's word.
screen: `THE TOP OF THE POLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: step off the pole. Even the top is a place to let go of. That's the week.

chat.meaning: The one on top has got somewhere, but not yet the real thing. Stepping off isn't throwing practice away; it's letting go of the height.
